Volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × 38.50 × 10.5 (using πr² = 38.50 directly).
Volume = 404.25 ÷ 3 = 134.75cm³.

Q6. A conical tent is 8m high and its base is of 54dm radius. It is to be used to accommodate scouts. How many scouts can be accommodated in the tent if each scout requires 5.832m³ of air?

Convert the radius to metres: 54dm = 5.4m. Height h = 8m.
Volume of the tent = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 5.4² × 8 = (1/3) × (22/7) × 233.28 ≈ 244.39m³.
Number of scouts = 244.39 ÷ 5.832 ≈ 41.9.
So the tent can accommodate 41 scouts in full (about 42 scouts).
Note: The printed answer is 44 scouts, which is wrong: 244.39 ÷ 5.832 ≈ 41.9, so only 41 scouts (about 42) can be accommodated.

mcqs.q: For a cone, h = 8cm and slant height l = 10cm. Find the radius r.
For a cone, r = 3cm and h = 4cm. Find the slant height l.
mcqs.why: For a cone l^2 = r^2 + h^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so l = sqrt(25) = 5cm, the slant height of the cone.

mcqs.q: For a cone, r = 9cm and slant height l = 25cm. Find the height h.
Find the volume of a cone with r = 3cm and h = 4cm (pi = 22/7).
Find the volume of a cone with r = 7cm and h = 10cm (pi = 22/7).
A conical cup of radius 4cm and height 5cm is full of ice-cream. Find the quantity of ice-cream (pi = 22/7).
What is the total surface area of a solid cone of radius 3cm and height 4cm (pi = 22/7)?
mcqs.why: Slant height l = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5cm. Total surface area = (pi)r(r + l) = (22/7) x 3 x (3 + 5) = 528/7 = 75.428..., about 75.43cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the curved surface area of a cone with r = 6cm and slant height l = 10cm (pi = 22/7).
mcqs.why: Curved surface area = (pi)rl = (22/7) x 6 x 10 = 1320/7 = 188.571..., about 188.57cm^2 for this cone.

mcqs.q: The base area of a cone is 38.50cm^2 and its height is three times its radius. Find its volume.
A conical tent is 8m high with base radius 54dm. Each scout needs 5.832m^3 of air. How many scouts can it hold in full (pi = 22/7)?
mcqs.why: Radius = 54dm = 5.4m. Volume = (1/3) x (22/7) x 5.4^2 x 8 = 244.39m^3 approx. Scouts = 244.39/5.832 = 41.9 approx, so 41 scouts can be accommodated in full.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.7
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Find the volume and surface area of the following: (a) a square prism 10ft × 10ft × 32ft with a square pyramid on top whose slant height is 12ft (b) a rectangular prism 13cm long with a 6cm × 6cm end, with a pyramid on one end whose base is 6cm × 6cm and whose slant height is 11cm

(a) Volume of the prism = 10 × 10 × 32 = 3200ft³. For the pyramid, vertical height h: h² = 12² − 5² = 144 − 25 = 119 (half of the 10ft base is 5ft), so h = √119 ≈ 10.91ft. Volume of pyramid = (1/3) × 100 × 10.91 ≈ 363.62ft³. Total volume = 3200 + 363.62 = 3563.62ft³.
(a) Surface area: 4 prism walls = 4 × (10 × 32) = 1280ft²; bottom = 10 × 10 = 100ft² (the top of the prism is covered by the pyramid base and is not counted); pyramid lateral area = 4 × (1/2 × 10 × 12) = 240ft². Total surface area = 1280 + 100 + 240 = 1620ft².
(b) Volume of the prism = 13 × 6 × 6 = 468cm³. For the pyramid, vertical height h: h² = 11² − 3² = 121 − 9 = 112 (half of the 6cm base is 3cm), so h = √112 ≈ 10.58cm. Volume of pyramid = (1/3) × 36 × 10.58 ≈ 127cm³. Total volume = 468 + 127 = 595cm³.
(b) Surface area: 4 prism walls = 4 × (13 × 6) = 312cm²; the far end = 6 × 6 = 36cm² (the near end is covered by the pyramid base); pyramid lateral area = 4 × (1/2 × 6 × 11) = 132cm². Total surface area = 312 + 36 + 132 = 480cm².
Note: The printed volumes 363.62ft³ for (a) and 127cm³ for (b) are the volumes of the pyramids only — the prism volumes (3200ft³ and 468cm³) were left out. The correct total volumes are 3563.62ft³ and 595cm³. The printed surface areas 1620ft² and 480cm² are correct.

Q2. Determine the volume of the composite objects shown below: (a) a rectangular prism 6.7cm long, 2.9cm wide and 2.9cm high with a pyramid of vertical height 2.1cm on top, the pyramid base being 6.7cm × 2.9cm (b) a tree: a cylindrical trunk of diameter 1.5ft and height 8ft with a spherical canopy of diameter 9ft

(a) Volume of prism = 6.7 × 2.9 × 2.9 = 56.35cm³ (6.7 × 2.9 = 19.43; 19.43 × 2.9 = 56.347).
(a) Volume of pyramid = (1/3) × base area × height = (1/3) × (6.7 × 2.9) × 2.1 = (1/3) × 19.43 × 2.1 = 13.60cm³.
(a) Total volume = 56.35 + 13.60 = 69.95cm³ (approx).
(b) Trunk: radius = 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75ft. Volume of cylinder = πr²h = 3.14 × 0.75² × 8 = 3.14 × 4.5 = 14.13ft³ (taking π ≈ 3.14).
(b) Canopy: radius = 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5ft. Volume of sphere = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 4.5³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 91.125 = 381.51ft³.
(b) Total volume = 14.13 + 381.51 = 395.64ft³.
Note: The printed answers are wrong: for (a) 13.6cm³ is the volume of the pyramid only (the prism's 56.35cm³ was left out; correct total ≈ 69.95cm³), and for (b) 109.44ft³ does not match a sphere of radius 4.5ft plus the trunk (correct total ≈ 395.64ft³).

Q3. The composite object in the illustration, at right, consists of a hemisphere connected to the top of a cone. The common diameter is 300mm and the height of the cone is 200mm. Find the object's: a. Surface area (in cm²) b. Volume (in cm³)

Convert to cm: diameter = 300mm = 30cm, so radius r = 15cm. Cone height = 200mm = 20cm. Take π ≈ 3.14 (as in the answer key).
Slant height of the cone: l² = r² + h² = 15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625, so l = 25cm.
a. Surface area = Curved surface of hemisphere + curved surface of cone (the joining circle is inside and is not counted) = 2πr² + πrl.
a. = 2 × 3.14 × 15² + 3.14 × 15 × 25 = 1413 + 1177.5 = 2590.5cm² ≈ 2590cm².
b. Volume = Volume of hemisphere + volume of cone = (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h.
b. = (2/3) × 3.14 × 3375 + (1/3) × 3.14 × 225 × 20 = 7065 + 4710 = 11775cm³.

Q4. The composite object in the illustration, at right, consists of two hemispheres which are connected by a cylinder in between. The diameter is 2 feet and the length of the cylinder is 6 feet. Find the object's: a. Surface Area b. Volume

Diameter = 2 feet, so radius r = 1 foot. The two hemispheres together make one full sphere. Take π ≈ 22/7 (as in the answer key).
a. Surface Area = Curved surface of cylinder + surface area of the sphere formed by the two hemispheres = 2πrh + 4πr².
a. = 2 × (22/7) × 1 × 6 + 4 × (22/7) × 1² = 264/7 + 88/7 = 352/7 ≈ 50.29 feet².
b. Volume = Volume of cylinder + volume of the sphere = πr²h + (4/3)πr³.
b. = (22/7) × 1 × 6 + (4/3) × (22/7) × 1 = 18.86 + 4.19 ≈ 23.05 feet³.
Note: The printed answers give the units as cm² and cm³ although the figure is in feet, and the printed volume 10.48 is wrong: with r = 1 foot and cylinder length 6 feet the correct volume is about 23.05 feet³. The printed surface area 50.29 is correct in value (in feet²).

mcqs.q: A square prism 10ft x 10ft x 32ft has a square pyramid on top with slant height 12ft. Find the total volume.
mcqs.why: Prism volume = 10 x 10 x 32 = 3200. Pyramid height: h^2 = 12^2 - 5^2 = 119, h = 10.91 approx, so pyramid volume = (1/3) x 100 x 10.91 = 363.62 approx. Total = 3200 + 363.62 = 3563.62 cubic feet.

mcqs.q: For the same solid (square prism 10ft x 10ft x 32ft with a square pyramid, slant height 12ft, on top), find the total surface area.
mcqs.why: Prism walls = 4 x (10 x 32) = 1280; bottom = 10 x 10 = 100 (the top is covered by the pyramid base); pyramid faces = 4 x (1/2 x 10 x 12) = 240. Total = 1280 + 100 + 240 = 1620 square feet.

mcqs.q: A rectangular prism 13cm long with a 6cm x 6cm end has a pyramid (base 6cm x 6cm, slant height 11cm) on one end. Find the total volume.
mcqs.why: Prism volume = 13 x 6 x 6 = 468cm^3. Pyramid height: h^2 = 11^2 - 3^2 = 112, h = 10.58 approx, so pyramid volume = (1/3) x 36 x 10.58 = 127 approx. Total = 468 + 127 = 595cm^3.

mcqs.q: For the same solid (rectangular prism 13cm x 6cm x 6cm with a pyramid of slant height 11cm on one end), find the total surface area.
mcqs.why: Prism walls = 4 x (13 x 6) = 312cm^2; far end = 6 x 6 = 36cm^2 (the near end is covered); pyramid faces = 4 x (1/2 x 6 x 11) = 132cm^2. Total = 312 + 36 + 132 = 480cm^2.

mcqs.q: A rectangular prism 6.7cm x 2.9cm x 2.9cm has a pyramid of vertical height 2.1cm on top, with base 6.7cm x 2.9cm. Find the total volume.
A tree has a cylindrical trunk of diameter 1.5ft and height 8ft, and a spherical canopy of diameter 9ft. Find the total volume (pi = 3.14).
A hemisphere sits on top of a cone; their common diameter is 300mm and the cone height is 200mm. Find the slant height of the cone.
mcqs.why: Convert: radius r = 30/2 = 15cm and cone height h = 20cm. Slant height: l^2 = r^2 + h^2 = 15^2 + 20^2 = 225 + 400 = 625, so l = sqrt(625) = 25cm.

mcqs.q: For that hemisphere-on-cone solid (radius 15cm, cone height 20cm, slant height 25cm), find the surface area (pi = 3.14).
mcqs.why: Surface area = curved hemisphere + curved cone = 2(pi)r^2 + (pi)rl = 2 x 3.14 x 15^2 + 3.14 x 15 x 25 = 1413 + 1177.5 = 2590.5cm^2; the joining circle is inside and not counted.

mcqs.q: For that hemisphere-on-cone solid (radius 15cm, cone height 20cm), find the volume (pi = 3.14).
mcqs.why: Volume = hemisphere + cone = (2/3) x 3.14 x 15^3 + (1/3) x 3.14 x 15^2 x 20 = 7065 + 4710 = 11775cm^3 for the composite solid.

mcqs.q: Two hemispheres are joined by a cylinder between them; diameter 2 feet and cylinder length 6 feet. Find the total volume (pi = 22/7).
mcqs.why: Radius r = 1 foot; the two hemispheres make one sphere. Volume = cylinder + sphere = (22/7) x 1^2 x 6 + (4/3) x (22/7) x 1^3 = 18.86 + 4.19 = 23.05 cubic feet approx.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Which shapes are congruent and which are similar? (Figure shows shapes labelled A, B, C, D, E, F, J, K, L, M, N, P, Q, R, S, T, U, including pentagons A and Q, parallelograms C and F, cylinders S and U, block-and-cylinder solids P, Q, R and M, composite shapes B and L, arrows E and J, right triangles D and T, and diamonds K and N)

Congruent shapes have exactly the same shape and the same size; similar shapes have the same shape but not necessarily the same size (book, section 4.1). Compare each pair of the same kind of shape in the figure.
Congruent pairs (same shape and same size): C and F (parallelograms); P and Q (block-and-cylinder solids); M and R (block-and-cylinder solids); B and L (composite shapes).
Similar pairs (same shape, different size): S and U (cylinders); A and Q (pentagons); E and J (arrows); D and T (right angled triangles); K and N (diamonds).
These are exactly the pairs given in the book's answer key.
Note: The figure uses the letter Q twice — once for a block-and-cylinder solid (congruent to P) and once for a pentagon (similar to A).

Q2. If △ADC ≅ △ABC, then write the name of pairs of congruent angles and congruent sides also write the case of congruency. (Figure: AB and AD carry the same tick marks, BC and DC carry the same tick marks, and AC is the common side)

From the tick marks in the figure: side AB ≅ side AD, and side BC ≅ side DC.
Side AC is common to both triangles, so AC ≅ AC.
Thus all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal, so △ADC ≅ △ABC by the SSS ≅ SSS case of congruency.
Congruent sides: AB ≅ AD; BC ≅ DC (printed as BC ≅ CD); AC ≅ AC.
Congruent angles (corresponding angles of congruent triangles): ∠BAC ≅ ∠DAC; ∠ABC ≅ ∠ADC; ∠ACB ≅ ∠ACD.

Q3. In the adjoining figure, a parallelogram ABCD and four triangles AOD, DOC, COB, AOB are shown (O is the intersection of the diagonals AC and BD). Which pairs of these triangles appear to be congruent? State the case of congruency.

In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so OA ≅ OC and OB ≅ OD, and opposite sides are equal: AB ≅ CD and AD ≅ BC.
△AOD and △COB: AD ≅ BC (opposite sides), OA ≅ OC and OD ≅ OB (diagonals bisect each other) — also ∠AOD ≅ ∠COB (vertically opposite angles). So △AOD ≅ △COB by SSS (or SAS) congruency. (The answer key pairs △AOD with △BOC, the same triangle.)
△AOB and △COD: AB ≅ CD (opposite sides), OA ≅ OC and OB ≅ OD — also ∠AOB ≅ ∠COD (vertically opposite angles). So △AOB ≅ △COD by SSS (or SAS) congruency. (The answer key pairs △AOB with △DOC, the same triangle.)
So the congruent pairs are △AOD ≅ △COB and △AOB ≅ △COD.

Q4. Given that m∠B = m∠M, then prove that the triangles shown are congruent. (Figure: right angled △ABC with the right angle at C, and right angled △MNL with the right angle at N; the hypotenuses AB and ML carry the same tick mark, and BC and MN carry the same tick marks)

In △ABC and △MNL (written in the correspondence A ↔ L, B ↔ M, C ↔ N):
From the tick marks in the figure: hypotenuse AB ≅ hypotenuse ML, and side BC ≅ side MN.
It is given that m∠B = m∠M, and this angle is the included angle between the sides AB, BC in △ABC and between the sides ML, MN in △MNL.
Therefore △ABC ≅ △MNL by the SAS ≅ SAS case of congruency (two sides and the included angle).
Consequently the remaining corresponding parts are also equal, e.g. AC ≅ LN (as listed in the answer key, which also lists BC ≅ MN).

mcqs.q: What does it mean for two shapes to be congruent?
options: They have the same shape but different sizes
They have the same size but different shapes
They have the same area but different shapes
They have exactly the same shape and the same size
mcqs.why: By the notes, congruent shapes have exactly the same shape and the same size, while similar shapes keep the shape but may change size.

mcqs.q: What does it mean for two shapes to be similar?
options: They have the same shape but not necessarily the same size
They have exactly the same shape and the same size
They have different shapes and different sizes
They have the same perimeter but different shapes
mcqs.why: By the notes, similar shapes have the same shape but not necessarily the same size, unlike congruent shapes which also match in size.

mcqs.q: In the figure of Exercise 4.1, which pair is a congruent pair?
mcqs.why: The notes list C and F as congruent parallelograms with the same shape and size, while S and U, A and Q, and E and J are listed as similar pairs of different size.

mcqs.q: In the figure of Exercise 4.1, which pair is a similar pair?
mcqs.why: The notes list S and U as similar cylinders with the same shape but different size, while C and F, B and L, and P and Q are listed as congruent pairs.

mcqs.q: If triangle ADC is congruent to triangle ABC with AB marked equal to AD and BC marked equal to DC, and AC common, which congruency case applies?
mcqs.why: All three pairs of corresponding sides are equal: AB = AD, BC = DC and AC = AC (common side), so the case is SSS, side-side-side.

mcqs.q: In triangle ADC congruent to triangle ABC, which angle is congruent to angle BAC?
mcqs.why: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal: angle BAC corresponds to angle DAC, angle ABC to angle ADC, and angle ACB to angle ACD.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD meet at O. Which pair of triangles is congruent?
options: Triangle AOD and triangle AOB only
Triangle DOC and triangle AOD only
No triangles in the figure are congruent
mcqs.why: Diagonals bisect each other so OA = OC and OD = OB, and AD = BC as opposite sides, giving triangle AOD congruent to triangle COB by SSS.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram ABCD with diagonals meeting at O, which pair of triangles is congruent?
options: Triangle AOB and triangle AOD only
Triangle COB and triangle AOB only
Triangle AOD and triangle DOC only
mcqs.why: AB = CD as opposite sides and OA = OC, OB = OD because diagonals bisect each other, so triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD by SSS.

mcqs.q: Why are angle AOD and angle COB equal in the parallelogram figure?
options: They are corresponding angles on parallel lines
They are alternate angles on parallel lines
They are angles in the same segment
mcqs.why: Angles AOD and COB are formed by the two intersecting diagonals AC and BD at O, so they are vertically opposite angles and therefore equal.

mcqs.q: Right triangles ABC and MNL have hypotenuse AB equal to hypotenuse ML, side BC equal to side MN, and angle B equal to angle M. By which case are they congruent?
mcqs.why: Two sides AB, BC and ML, MN are equal and angle B = angle M is the included angle between them, so the triangles are congruent by SAS.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Construction of Triangles and Transformation

lessons.title: Exercise 4.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Construct a square ABCD, when a diagonal mAC = 4.5cm.

In a square both diagonals are equal and they bisect each other at right angles (method of book Example 5).
Step 1: Draw the diagonal AC = 4.5cm.
Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AC, meeting AC at its midpoint O.
Step 3: With centre O and radius OA (= 2.25cm, half of the diagonal), draw arcs on the perpendicular bisector on both sides of AC, cutting it at B and D, so that BD = 4.5cm and O is also the midpoint of BD.
Step 4: Join A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A.
Then ABCD is the required square with diagonal 4.5cm.

Q2. Construct a square PQRS, when its diagonal is 4cm more than its side.

Use the book's method for a square when the difference between its diagonal and side is given (Example 6), here with difference 4cm.
Step 1: Draw a line PQ and mark a point A on it.
Step 2: Construct ∠QAN = 90° at A, with one arm along the line and the other arm AN upwards.
Step 3: With centre A and radius 4cm, draw arcs cutting the first arm at M and the arm AN at L, so AM = AL = 4cm.
Step 4: Join L to M. With centre M and radius equal to LM, draw an arc cutting the first arm, produced, at the point B; then AB is the side of the required square (because AB − AM = LM gives diagonal − side = 4cm).
Step 5: With centre A and radius AB, draw an arc cutting AN at D.
Step 6: With radius AB, draw one arc with centre B and another arc with centre D; the two arcs intersect at C.
Step 7: Join C to D and C to B, and rename the vertices in order as P, Q, R, S.
Then PQRS is the required square, whose diagonal is 4cm more than its side.

Q3. Construct a square PQRS, when the sum of the diagonal and a side of the square is 8cm.

Use the book's method for a square when the sum of its diagonal and side is given (Example 7), here with sum 8cm.
Step 1: Draw a line and mark a point S on it; call the line SQ.
Step 2: Construct ∠QSR = 90° at S.
Step 3: With centre S and radius 8cm, draw an arc cutting SR at L, and another arc of radius 8cm cutting SQ at A, so SL = SA = 8cm.
Step 4: Join L to A. With centre S and radius equal to AL, draw an arc cutting SQ at B; then AB is the side of the required square (because the part SB equals the diagonal, and AB = sum − diagonal = side).
Step 5: Draw a perpendicular at B to SQ and mark it BM.
Step 6: With centre B and radius AB, draw an arc cutting BM at C.
Step 7: With radius AB, draw one arc with centre A and another arc with centre C; the two arcs intersect at D.
Step 8: Join C to D and D to A, and rename the vertices in order as P, Q, R, S.
Then PQRS is the required square, whose diagonal plus side equals 8cm.

Q4. Construct a rectangle ABCD, when mAB = 4cm and mBC = 6cm.

Use the book's method for a rectangle when two sides are given (Example 8).
Step 1: Draw AB = 4cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠A = ∠B = 90° at A and at B, and draw the rays AG and BH upwards.
Step 3: With centre A and radius 6cm, draw an arc cutting AG at D.
Step 4: With centre B and radius 6cm, draw an arc cutting BH at C.
Step 5: Join C to D.
Then ABCD is the required rectangle with AB = 4cm and BC = 6cm.

Q5. Construct a rectangle ABCD, when mAB = 5.5cm and mAC = 8cm.

Use the book's method for a rectangle when a side and the diagonal are given (Example 9): AB = 5.5cm, diagonal AC = 8cm.
Step 1: Draw AB = 5.5cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠A = ∠B = 90° at A and at B, and draw the rays AX and BY upwards.
Step 3: With centre A and radius 8cm (the diagonal), draw an arc cutting BY at C, so that AC = 8cm.
Step 4: With centre B and radius 8cm, draw an arc cutting AX at D (the second diagonal BD is also 8cm, since the diagonals of a rectangle are equal).
Step 5: Join C to D.
Then ABCD is the required rectangle.

Q6. Construct a rhombus KLMN, when the mKL = 5cm, m∠K = 75°.

Use the book's method for a rhombus when one side and the base angle are given (Example 10).
Step 1: Draw KL = 5cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠K = 75° at K and draw the ray KX.
Step 3: With centre K and radius 5cm, draw an arc cutting KX at N (so KN = 5cm, since all sides of a rhombus are equal).
Step 4: With centre N and radius 5cm, draw an arc above the figure.
Step 5: With centre L and radius 5cm, draw an arc cutting the previous arc at M.
Step 6: Join M to N and M to L.
Then KLMN is the required rhombus.

Q7. Construct a rhombus STUV, when mST = 6cm and mSU = 9cm.

Here SU is a diagonal of the rhombus. Use the book's method for a rhombus when one side and a diagonal are given (Example 11).
Step 1: Draw ST = 6cm.
Step 2: With centre S and radius 9cm, draw an arc (this will locate U at distance SU = 9cm from S).
Step 3: With centre T and radius 6cm, draw an arc cutting the previous arc at U.
Step 4: With centre U and radius 6cm, draw an arc.
Step 5: With centre S and radius 6cm, draw an arc cutting the previous arc at V.
Step 6: Join T to U, U to V and S to V.
Then STUV is the required rhombus with side 6cm and diagonal 9cm.

Q8. Construct a parallelogram ABCD with diagonals 6cm and 8cm and the angle between them is 70°.

The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Use the book's method (Example 12).
Step 1: Draw the diagonal AC = 6cm.
Step 2: Bisect AC and call its midpoint O, so OA = OC = 3cm.
Step 3: Construct an angle of 70° at O on AC and produce the line on both sides of AC.
Step 4: The second diagonal is 8cm, so its half is 4cm. With centre O and radius 4cm, draw arcs on the line of Step 3 on both sides of AC, cutting it at B and D, so OB = OD = 4cm and BD = 8cm.
Step 5: Join A to B and A to D.
Step 6: Join C to B and C to D.
Then ABCD is the required parallelogram.

Q9. Construct a parallelogram DEFG where mDE = 5.5cm, mEF = 6.5cm and m∠E = 60°.

∠E is the included angle between the sides DE and EF. Use the book's method for a parallelogram when two adjacent sides and the included angle are given (Example 13).
Step 1: Draw DE = 5.5cm, keeping E at the right-hand end.
Step 2: Construct ∠DEF = 60° at E and draw the ray EX upwards.
Step 3: With centre E and radius 6.5cm, draw an arc cutting EX at F, so EF = 6.5cm.
Step 4: With centre D and radius 6.5cm, draw an arc above D.
Step 5: With centre F and radius 5.5cm, draw an arc cutting the previous arc at G.
Step 6: Join G to F and G to D.
Then DEFG is the required parallelogram.

Q10. Construct a kite DEFG where mDE = 4cm, mEF = 8cm and the length of the longer diagonal is mDE = 10cm (as printed).

Use the book's method for a kite when two unequal sides and a diagonal are given (Example 14): the two unequal adjacent sides are 4cm and 8cm and the longer diagonal joining their opposite vertices is 10cm.
Step 1: Draw DE = 4cm.
Step 2: With centre E and radius 8cm, draw an arc.
Step 3: With centre D and radius 10cm (the longer diagonal), draw an arc cutting the previous arc at F.
Step 4: With centre D and radius 4cm, draw an arc above D.
Step 5: With centre F and radius 8cm, draw an arc cutting the previous arc at G.
Step 6: Join F to E, F to G and D to G.
Then DEFG is the required kite.
Note: The question prints the longer diagonal as mDE = 10cm, but DE is already the side of 4cm; following the pattern of the book's Example 14 the longer diagonal must be DF = 10cm, which is what is constructed above.

Q11. Draw a trapezium EFGH so that FE ∥ GH, m∠E = 70°, mEF = 8cm, mEH = 5cm, mHG = 4cm.

Use the book's method for a trapezium when three sides and one angle are given and one pair of sides is parallel (Example 16).
Step 1: Draw the base EF = 8cm.
Step 2: At E, construct an angle of 70° with a protractor and draw the ray EP.
Step 3: With centre E and radius 5cm, draw an arc cutting EP at H, so EH = 5cm.
Step 4: With ruler and set square, draw through H a ray HQ parallel to EF.
Step 5: With centre H and radius 4cm, draw an arc cutting HQ at G, so HG = 4cm.
Step 6: Join H to G (already on the ray) and join G to F.
Then EFGH is the required trapezium with FE ∥ GH.

Q12. Draw a trapezium PQRS in which mPQ = 7cm, mQR = mRS = 5cm, mPS = 6cm.

PQRS has RS ∥ PQ (the two bases). Use the book's method for a trapezium when four sides are given (Example 15).
Step 1: Draw the base PQ = 7cm.
Step 2: Mark a point E on PQ such that PE = RS = 5cm.
Step 3: With centre E and radius 6cm (= PS), draw an arc.
Step 4: With centre Q and radius 5cm (= QR), draw an arc cutting the previous arc at R.
Step 5: With centre R and radius 5cm, draw an arc.
Step 6: With centre P and radius 6cm (= PS), draw an arc cutting the previous arc at S.
Step 7: Join Q to R, R to S and P to S.
Then PQRS is the required trapezium.

mcqs.q: To construct a square with diagonal AC = 4.5 cm, what radius is used from the midpoint O of AC to mark B and D?
mcqs.why: Half of the diagonal = 4.5 / 2 = 2.25 cm, so OA = 2.25 cm is the radius used from centre O to cut the perpendicular bisector at B and D.

mcqs.q: In a square, how do the diagonals behave, as used in constructing a square from its diagonal?
options: They are equal but never bisect each other
They bisect each other but are never at right angles
They are equal and bisect each other at right angles
One diagonal is twice the other diagonal
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a square both diagonals are equal and they bisect each other at right angles, which is the basis of the construction.

mcqs.q: A rectangle ABCD is constructed with AB = 4 cm and BC = 6 cm. What angles are constructed at A and B first?
mcqs.why: Every angle of a rectangle is a right angle, so angles of 90 degrees are constructed at A and at B before marking D and C at distance 6 cm.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has side AB = 5.5 cm and diagonal AC = 8 cm. With centre A, what radius cuts the ray from B to locate C?
mcqs.why: C lies at the diagonal distance from A, so radius = AC = 8 cm. The second diagonal BD is also 8 cm because rectangle diagonals are equal.

mcqs.q: A rhombus KLMN has side KL = 5 cm and angle K = 75 degrees. Why is KN also marked as 5 cm?
options: Diagonals of a rhombus are equal
Opposite angles of a rhombus are equal
All sides of a rhombus are equal
Each diagonal bisects a vertex angle
mcqs.why: All sides of a rhombus are equal, so KN = KL = 5 cm, and arcs of radius 5 cm from N and L then meet at M to complete the rhombus.

mcqs.q: A rhombus STUV has side ST = 6 cm and diagonal SU = 9 cm. To locate U from T, what radius is used with centre T?
mcqs.why: U is one side-length from T, so radius = ST = 6 cm with centre T cuts the arc of radius SU = 9 cm from S at the point U.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm with 70 degrees between them. If AC = 6 cm is drawn first, what are OA and OC?
mcqs.why: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so OA = OC = 6 / 2 = 3 cm, while the halves of the 8 cm diagonal are 8 / 2 = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm. What length is marked from the midpoint O along the 70-degree line to locate B and D?
mcqs.why: Half of the second diagonal = 8 / 2 = 4 cm, so OB = OD = 4 cm are marked from O on both sides to give BD = 8 cm in total.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram DEFG has DE = 5.5 cm, EF = 6.5 cm and angle E = 60 degrees. What is angle E called in this construction?
options: The included angle between sides DE and EF
mcqs.why: Angle E is formed by the two given adjacent sides DE and EF meeting at E, so it is their included angle of 60 degrees.

mcqs.q: Trapezium EFGH has FE parallel to GH, angle E = 70 degrees, EF = 8 cm, EH = 5 cm and HG = 4 cm. How is the ray through H drawn?
options: At 70 degrees to EF at H
As the perpendicular bisector of EF
Parallel to EF using ruler and set square
mcqs.why: Since FE is parallel to GH, the ray through H must be drawn parallel to EF, and then HG = 4 cm is marked along that parallel ray.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Without construction check, whether or not a triangle can be constructed with given sides. If the answer is negative, give reason. (i) 8cm, 5cm, 2cm (ii) 6cm, 3.5cm, 2cm (iii) 6.7cm, 4.5cm, 3.4cm (iv) 9cm, 4.5cm, 2.8cm (v) 7cm, 5.4cm, 3.5cm (vi) 8.8cm, 3.6cm, 5.2cm

Rule (book, Remember box): the sum of the measures of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the measure of its third side. It is enough to check the two smaller sides against the largest side.
(i) 5 + 2 = 7, which is less than 8. So a triangle can NOT be constructed, because the sum of the two smaller sides (7cm) is less than the third side (8cm).
(ii) 3.5 + 2 = 5.5, which is less than 6. So a triangle can NOT be constructed, because the sum of the two smaller sides (5.5cm) is less than the third side (6cm).
(iii) 4.5 + 3.4 = 7.9, which is greater than 6.7 (and the other two sums are also greater). So a triangle CAN be constructed.
(iv) 4.5 + 2.8 = 7.3, which is less than 9. So a triangle can NOT be constructed, because the sum of the two smaller sides (7.3cm) is less than the third side (9cm).
(v) 5.4 + 3.5 = 8.9, which is greater than 7 (and the other two sums are also greater). So a triangle CAN be constructed.
(vi) 3.6 + 5.2 = 8.8, which is equal to 8.8, not greater. So a triangle can NOT be constructed, because the sum of the two smaller sides must be strictly greater than the third side; here it is only equal, so the three points would lie on one straight line.

Q2. Construct the following triangles with the help of pair of compasses and a ruler when the measure of the two sides and their included angle is given: (i) 60°, 8.4cm, 5.5cm (ii) 45°, 7.5cm, 4.2cm (iii) 30°, 6.8cm, 4.6cm (iv) 120°, 5.4cm, 3.6cm

Use the book's SAS method (Example 18) in each case: draw one side, construct the included angle at one end, mark the second side on the new ray, and join.
(i) Included angle 60°, sides 8.4cm and 5.5cm: Draw AB = 8.4cm. Construct ∠BAK = 60° at A. With centre A and radius 5.5cm, draw an arc cutting AK at C. Join C to B. △ABC is the required triangle.
(ii) Included angle 45°, sides 7.5cm and 4.2cm: Draw AB = 7.5cm. Construct ∠BAK = 45° at A. With centre A and radius 4.2cm, draw an arc cutting AK at C. Join C to B. △ABC is the required triangle.
(iii) Included angle 30°, sides 6.8cm and 4.6cm: Draw AB = 6.8cm. Construct ∠BAK = 30° at A. With centre A and radius 4.6cm, draw an arc cutting AK at C. Join C to B. △ABC is the required triangle.
(iv) Included angle 120°, sides 5.4cm and 3.6cm: Draw AB = 5.4cm. Construct ∠BAK = 120° at A. With centre A and radius 3.6cm, draw an arc cutting AK at C. Join C to B. △ABC is the required triangle.

Q3. Construct an isosceles triangle, in which the measure of the two congruent sides is 6.4cm each and measure of their included angle is 30°.

This is the SAS case with the two sides equal.
Step 1: Draw a side AB = 6.4cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠BAK = 30° at A (the included angle between the two congruent sides).
Step 3: With centre A and radius 6.4cm, draw an arc cutting AK at C, so AC = 6.4cm = AB.
Step 4: Join C to B.
Then △ABC is the required isosceles triangle with AB ≅ AC and included angle 30°.

Q4. Construct the following triangles with the help of a ruler and a protractor. (i) △ABC, when mAB = 5.8cm, mBC = 3.6cm and m∠B = 30° (ii) △PQR, when mPQ = 4.8cm, mQR = 4.8cm and m∠Q = 120°

In each triangle the given angle is the included angle between the two given sides, so this is again the SAS case, with the angle drawn by protractor.
(i) Draw AB = 5.8cm. At B, use the protractor to construct ∠ABX = 30°. With centre B and radius 3.6cm, draw an arc (or measure 3.6cm with the ruler) cutting BX at C, so BC = 3.6cm. Join C to A. △ABC is the required triangle.
(ii) Draw PQ = 4.8cm. At Q, use the protractor to construct ∠PQX = 120°. Measure QR = 4.8cm along QX and mark the point R. Join R to P. △PQR is the required (isosceles) triangle.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 8 cm, 5 cm and 2 cm?
options: Yes, because every sum of two sides exceeds the third
mcqs.why: Check the two smaller sides against the largest: 5 + 2 = 7, and 7 < 8, so the triangle inequality fails and no triangle can be formed.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 6.7 cm, 4.5 cm and 3.4 cm?
mcqs.why: Check the two smaller sides: 4.5 + 3.4 = 7.9, and 7.9 > 6.7, so the triangle inequality holds and a triangle can be constructed.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 8.8 cm, 3.6 cm and 5.2 cm?
options: No, because 3.6 + 5.2 = 8.8 is only equal to the third side, not greater
Yes, because equality is enough for a triangle
mcqs.why: The sum must be strictly greater: 3.6 + 5.2 = 8.8, which equals the third side 8.8, so the points lie on one straight line and no triangle forms.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 9 cm, 4.5 cm and 2.8 cm?
mcqs.why: Check the two smaller sides against the largest: 4.5 + 2.8 = 7.3, and 7.3 < 9, so the triangle inequality fails and no triangle can be formed.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 7 cm, 5.4 cm and 3.5 cm?
mcqs.why: Check the two smaller sides: 5.4 + 3.5 = 8.9, and 8.9 > 7, so the triangle inequality holds and a triangle can be constructed.

mcqs.q: What is the triangle inequality rule used to check whether a triangle can be constructed?
options: The sum of any two sides is always greater than the third side
The sum of any two sides equals the third side
The sum of any two sides is always less than the third side
The longest side equals the sum of the other two sides
mcqs.why: The Remember box states the sum of the measures of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the measure of its third side.

mcqs.q: A triangle is constructed with included angle 60 degrees and sides 8.4 cm and 5.5 cm. Which construction case is this?
options: ASA case: two angles and included side
SAS case: two sides and their included angle
HS case: hypotenuse and one side given
mcqs.why: The given angle of 60 degrees lies between the two given sides 8.4 cm and 5.5 cm, so the construction uses the SAS method of Example 18.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has two congruent sides of 6.4 cm each with included angle 30 degrees. After drawing AB = 6.4 cm and the 30-degree angle at A, how is C located?
options: With centre B and radius 6.4 cm, an arc cuts the base at C
With centre A and radius 3.2 cm, an arc cuts the new ray at C
With centre A and radius 6.4 cm, an arc cuts the new ray at C
By measuring 30 cm along the new ray from A
mcqs.why: The second congruent side AC must equal AB = 6.4 cm, so an arc with centre A and radius 6.4 cm cuts the 30-degree ray at C, giving AC = 6.4 cm.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has AB = 5.8 cm, BC = 3.6 cm and angle B = 30 degrees. Why is this an SAS construction?
options: Angle B is opposite side AB
Sides AB and BC do not meet at B
Angle B is the included side between two angles
Angle B is the included angle between sides AB and BC
mcqs.why: Sides AB and BC both meet at vertex B, so angle B = 30 degrees is included between them, making this the SAS case drawn with ruler and protractor.

mcqs.q: Triangle PQR has PQ = 4.8 cm, QR = 4.8 cm and angle Q = 120 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?
mcqs.why: Two sides are equal, PQ = QR = 4.8 cm, so the triangle has a pair of congruent sides and is isosceles, with the included angle 120 degrees at Q.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.4
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Construct the following triangles with the help of a compass and a ruler (base angles and base given — ASA case): (i) base angles 30°, 45°, base 6.5cm (ii) base angles 45°, 90°, base 5.4cm (iii) base angles 30°, 120°, base 4.8cm (iv) base angles 45°, 60°, base 3.6cm

Use the book's ASA method (Example 19) in each case: draw the base BC, construct one base angle at B and the other at C, and let the two rays meet at A. The third angle can be checked as 180° minus the sum of the two base angles.
(i) Draw BC = 6.5cm. Construct ∠CBX = 30° at B and ∠BCY = 45° at C. BX and CY intersect at A. △ABC is the required triangle (third angle = 180° − 30° − 45° = 105°).
(ii) Draw BC = 5.4cm. Construct ∠CBX = 45° at B and ∠BCY = 90° at C. BX and CY intersect at A. △ABC is the required right angled triangle (third angle = 45°).
(iii) Draw BC = 4.8cm. Construct ∠CBX = 30° at B and ∠BCY = 120° at C. BX and CY intersect at A. △ABC is the required triangle (third angle = 30°).
(iv) Draw BC = 3.6cm. Construct ∠CBX = 45° at B and ∠BCY = 60° at C. BX and CY intersect at A. △ABC is the required triangle (third angle = 75°).

Q2. Construct an isosceles triangle. The length of its base is 8cm and the two angles on the base are of measure 45° each.

This is the ASA case with equal base angles, so the triangle is isosceles.
Step 1: Draw the base BC = 8cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠CBX = 45° at B.
Step 3: Construct ∠BCY = 45° at C.
Step 4: BX and CY intersect each other at the point A.
Then △ABC is the required isosceles triangle; its vertex angle is 180° − 45° − 45° = 90°.

Q3. Construct the following triangles by constructing angles with the help of a protractor. (i) △PQR, when m∠Q = 120°, m∠R = 30° and mQR = 5.3cm (ii) △GHK, when m∠G = 30°, m∠H = 60° and mGH = 4.5cm

In each case the given side is the included side between the two given angles (ASA), and the angles are drawn with a protractor.
(i) Draw QR = 5.3cm. At Q, construct ∠RQP = 120° with the protractor and draw the ray QP. At R, construct ∠QRP = 30° and draw the ray RP. The two rays intersect at P. △PQR is the required triangle (third angle ∠P = 30°).
(ii) Draw GH = 4.5cm. At G, construct ∠HGK = 30° with the protractor and draw the ray GK. At H, construct ∠GHK = 60° and draw the ray HK. The two rays intersect at K. △GHK is the required triangle (third angle ∠K = 90°).

Q4. Construct right angled triangles with the help of a compass. (i) Hypotenuse = 6.8cm, Base = 3.5cm (ii) Hypotenuse = 8.8cm, Base = 4.7cm (iii) Hypotenuse = 7.6cm, Base = 5.4cm (iv) Hypotenuse = 9cm, Altitude = 5cm

Use the book's HS method (Example 20) in each case: draw the given side, construct a 90° angle at one end, and cut the perpendicular ray with an arc of radius equal to the hypotenuse drawn from the other end.
(i) Draw BC = 3.5cm (base). Construct ∠CBX = 90° at B. With centre C and radius 6.8cm, draw an arc cutting BX at A. Join A to C. △ABC is the required right angled triangle.
(ii) Draw BC = 4.7cm (base). Construct ∠CBX = 90° at B. With centre C and radius 8.8cm, draw an arc cutting BX at A. Join A to C. △ABC is the required right angled triangle.
(iii) Draw BC = 5.4cm (base). Construct ∠CBX = 90° at B. With centre C and radius 7.6cm, draw an arc cutting BX at A. Join A to C. △ABC is the required right angled triangle.
(iv) Here the given side is the altitude. Draw BC = 5cm as the altitude. Construct ∠CBX = 90° at B. With centre C and radius 9cm (hypotenuse), draw an arc cutting BX at A. Join A to C. △ABC is the required right angled triangle with altitude 5cm and hypotenuse 9cm.

Q5. The measure of two sides of a triangle are 6.8cm and 4.4cm. If the angle opposite to the side of measure 6.8cm is a right angle, then construct the triangle.

The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is 6.8cm and the other given side, 4.4cm, is one leg. This is the HS case.
Step 1: Draw a line segment BC = 4.4cm (one side).
Step 2: Construct ∠CBX = 90° at B.
Step 3: With centre C and radius 6.8cm, draw an arc cutting BX at A.
Step 4: Join A to C.
Then △ABC is the required right angled triangle, with hypotenuse AC = 6.8cm opposite the right angle at B.

Q6. Construct △ABC, when mAB = 3.8cm, mAC = 5cm and m∠B = 90°.

Since ∠B = 90°, the side opposite it, AC = 5cm, is the hypotenuse, and AB = 3.8cm is one leg. This is the HS case.
Step 1: Draw AB = 3.8cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠ABX = 90° at B and draw the ray BX.
Step 3: With centre A and radius 5cm, draw an arc cutting BX at C, so that AC = 5cm.
Step 4: Join C to A (the arc point is already joined by the side AC).
Then △ABC is the required right angled triangle.

Q7. Construct △PQR, when mPQ = 4.6cm, mQR = 9.8cm and m∠Q = 90°.

∠Q is the included angle between the sides PQ and QR, so this is the SAS case with a right angle.
Step 1: Draw PQ = 4.6cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠PQX = 90° at Q and draw the ray QX.
Step 3: With centre Q and radius 9.8cm, draw an arc cutting QX at R, so QR = 9.8cm.
Step 4: Join R to P.
Then △PQR is the required right angled triangle (PR is its hypotenuse).

Q8. Draw angle bisectors of any suitable size of a triangle.

Follow the book's steps for the angle bisector of a triangle (the three bisectors meet at the incentre).
Step 1: Draw any triangle ABC of a suitable size.
Step 2: With centre A and any suitable radius, draw an arc cutting AC and AB at X and Y respectively.
Step 3: With centre X draw an arc inside the angle, and with centre Y and the same radius draw another arc cutting the first arc at Z.
Step 4: Join A to Z and produce it to meet BC at L. Then AL is the angle bisector of ∠A.
Step 5: Repeat the same steps at B and at C to draw the bisectors BM and CN.
The three angle bisectors AL, BM and CN are concurrent; their meeting point O is the incentre of the triangle.

Q9. Draw side bisectors of any suitable size of a triangle.

Follow the book's steps for the perpendicular (side) bisector of a triangle (the three bisectors meet at the circumcentre).
Step 1: Draw any triangle ABC of a suitable size.
Step 2: With centre A and radius more than half of AB, draw two arcs, one above and one below AB.
Step 3: With centre B and the same radius, draw two arcs above and below AB, cutting the previous arcs at L and M.
Step 4: Join L to M. The line LM is the perpendicular bisector of the side AB.
Step 5: Repeat the same steps for the sides BC and AC to draw their perpendicular bisectors.
The three perpendicular bisectors are concurrent; their meeting point O is the circumcentre of the triangle.

Q10. Draw angle and perpendicular bisectors of any quadrilateral.

Take any quadrilateral ABCD of a suitable size and apply the same bisector constructions as for a triangle, once for the angles and once for the sides.
Step 1: Draw any quadrilateral ABCD.
Step 2 (angle bisectors): With centre A and any suitable radius, draw an arc cutting the two sides through A at two points. From those two points draw two equal arcs intersecting inside the angle, join A to the intersection point and produce the ray — this is the bisector of ∠A. Repeat at B, C and D for the other three angles.
Step 3 (perpendicular bisectors): For the side AB, draw arcs above and below AB with centre A and radius more than half of AB, then equal arcs with centre B cutting them at two points; join those two points to get the perpendicular bisector of AB. Repeat for BC, CD and DA.
The angle bisectors and the perpendicular bisectors of the quadrilateral are thus drawn; unlike a triangle, they need not all meet at a single point.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base angles 30 degrees and 45 degrees with base 6.5 cm. What is its third angle?
mcqs.why: Angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees: third angle = 180 - 30 - 45 = 180 - 75 = 105 degrees, as checked in the ASA construction.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base angles 45 degrees and 90 degrees with base 5.4 cm. What is its third angle?
mcqs.why: Angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees: third angle = 180 - 45 - 90 = 180 - 135 = 45 degrees, giving a right-angled triangle.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base 8 cm and base angles of 45 degrees each. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180 - 45 - 45 = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees, so the ASA construction with equal base angles gives a right angle at the vertex.

mcqs.q: Triangle PQR has angle Q = 120 degrees, angle R = 30 degrees and QR = 5.3 cm. What is angle P?
mcqs.why: Angles sum to 180 degrees: angle P = 180 - 120 - 30 = 180 - 150 = 30 degrees, with QR the included side in this ASA construction.

mcqs.q: Triangle GHK has angle G = 30 degrees, angle H = 60 degrees and GH = 4.5 cm. What is angle K?
mcqs.why: Angles sum to 180 degrees: angle K = 180 - 30 - 60 = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees, so triangle GHK is right-angled at K.

mcqs.q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 6.8 cm and base 3.5 cm. In the HS construction, what radius is used from C to cut the perpendicular ray?
mcqs.why: The arc must reach the hypotenuse length from C, so radius = hypotenuse = 6.8 cm cuts the 90-degree ray at B to locate vertex A.

mcqs.q: Two sides of a triangle are 6.8 cm and 4.4 cm, and the angle opposite the 6.8 cm side is a right angle. What is the 6.8 cm side?
mcqs.why: The side opposite a right angle is always the hypotenuse, so 6.8 cm is the hypotenuse and 4.4 cm is one leg in this HS construction.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has AB = 3.8 cm, AC = 5 cm and angle B = 90 degrees. Why is AC the hypotenuse?
options: AC is the longest side marked first
AC is adjacent to the right angle at B
AC is equal to AB in length
AC is opposite the right angle at B
mcqs.why: The side opposite the 90-degree angle at B is AC, so AC = 5 cm is the hypotenuse and AB = 3.8 cm is one leg in the HS case.

mcqs.q: What is the meeting point of the three angle bisectors of a triangle called?
mcqs.why: The notes state the three angle bisectors AL, BM and CN are concurrent and their meeting point O is the incentre of the triangle.

mcqs.q: What is the meeting point of the three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle called?
mcqs.why: The notes state the three perpendicular (side) bisectors are concurrent and their meeting point O is the circumcentre of the triangle.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.5
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Find the image of the shape shown after a rotation of 90° in the clockwise direction about the marked centre of rotation. (Figure: an L-shaped block standing above a marked centre of rotation below it)

In a rotation every point of the shape turns through the same angle about the centre of rotation, and the image is congruent to the original shape (book, section 4.5).
Step 1: Mark each corner of the L-shaped block and join every corner to the centre of rotation O with a straight line.
Step 2: For each corner, turn its joining line through 90° in the clockwise direction about O, keeping the same length (use a set square/protractor, or count squares on the grid: a point that is a squares right and b squares up from O moves to a point b squares right and a squares down from O, i.e. (x, y) → (y, −x) about O).
Step 3: Mark the new positions of all the corners and join them in the same order.
The image is the same L-shape turned on its side to the right of the centre: the long vertical part of the L now lies horizontally and the short foot of the L points upwards, and the whole image is congruent to the original block.

Q2. Rotate shape A anticlockwise through 90° about centre (1, 1). (Figure: shape A is the hexagon with vertices (1, 5), (6, 5), (6, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (1, 3), read from the grid)

Rotation through 90° anticlockwise (counterclockwise) about the centre C(1, 1): a point P(x, y) goes to P′ with P′ = C + (−(y − 1), (x − 1)), since about the origin the rule is (x, y) → (−y, x).
Vertex (1, 5): relative to C it is (0, 4) → (−4, 0), so the image is (1 − 4, 1 + 0) = (−3, 1).
Vertex (6, 5): relative (5, 4) → (−4, 5), image (1 − 4, 1 + 5) = (−3, 6).
Vertex (6, 1): relative (5, 0) → (0, 5), image (1, 6).
Vertex (4, 1): relative (3, 0) → (0, 3), image (1, 4).
Vertex (4, 3): relative (3, 2) → (−2, 3), image (−1, 4).
Vertex (1, 3): relative (0, 2) → (−2, 0), image (−1, 1).
So the image of shape A has vertices (−3, 1), (−3, 6), (1, 6), (1, 4), (−1, 4), (−1, 1), joined in that order; it is the same shape turned a quarter turn anticlockwise, lying to the left of the centre.

Q3. Rotate the shape drawn (a triangle on the grid) through 180° about the origin. (Vertices read from the printed grid as (0, −1), (−8, −2) and (−4, −5))

Rotation through 180° about the origin sends each point (x, y) to (−x, −y) (book: the image of P(x, y) under a half turn about the origin is P′(−x, −y)).
Vertex (0, −1) → (0, 1).
Vertex (−8, −2) → (8, 2).
Vertex (−4, −5) → (4, 5).
So the image triangle has vertices (0, 1), (8, 2) and (4, 5); it is the same triangle turned through a half turn, now above the x-axis. (Vertices were read from the printed grid, so each is correct to within one grid square.)

Q4. Rotate the shape drawn (a triangle on the grid) through 90° anticlockwise about the origin. (Vertices read from the printed grid as about (5, 7), (3, 2) and (8, 0))

Rotation through 90° anticlockwise (counterclockwise) about the origin sends each point (x, y) to (−y, x) (book, section 4.5).
Vertex (5, 7) → (−7, 5).
Vertex (3, 2) → (−2, 3).
Vertex (8, 0) → (0, 8).
So the image triangle has vertices (−7, 5), (−2, 3) and (0, 8), in the second quadrant. (Vertices were read from the printed grid, so each is correct to within about one grid square.)

Q5. Rotate the shape drawn (a quadrilateral on the grid) through 90° clockwise about the origin. (Vertices read from the printed grid as (−2, 3), (−8, 1), (−6, −2) and (−2, −2))

Rotation through 90° clockwise about the origin sends each point (x, y) to (y, −x) (book, section 4.5).
Vertex (−2, 3) → (3, 2).
Vertex (−8, 1) → (1, 8).
Vertex (−6, −2) → (−2, 6).
Vertex (−2, −2) → (−2, 2).
So the image quadrilateral has vertices (3, 2), (1, 8), (−2, 6) and (−2, 2), joined in that order.

Q6. State the coordinates of the image of the points under a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin: A(1, −2), B(0, 2), C(3, 2), D(3, −3)

Rule for a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin (book): (x, y) → (y, −x).
A(1, −2) → (−2, −1).
B(0, 2) → (2, 0).
C(3, 2) → (2, −3).
D(3, −3) → (−3, −3).
So A′(−2, −1), B′(2, 0), C′(2, −3) and D′(−3, −3).

Q7. State the coordinates of the image of the points under a rotation of 180° about the origin: P(−1, −5), Q(−1, 0), R(1, 1), S(3, −2)

Rule for a rotation of 180° about the origin (book): (x, y) → (−x, −y).
P(−1, −5) → (1, 5).
Q(−1, 0) → (1, 0).
R(1, 1) → (−1, −1).
S(3, −2) → (−3, 2).
So P′(1, 5), Q′(1, 0), R′(−1, −1) and S′(−3, 2).

Q8. Describe fully the transformation that maps shape QERN (vertices Q(−5, 0), E(−2, 0), R(−1, 3), N(−5, 5)) onto shape Q′E′R′N′ (vertices Q′(0, 5), E′(0, 2), R′(3, 1), N′(5, 5)).

Compare each point with its image: Q(−5, 0) → Q′(0, 5); E(−2, 0) → E′(0, 2); R(−1, 3) → R′(3, 1); N(−5, 5) → N′(5, 5).
In every case the new x-coordinate equals the old y-coordinate, and the new y-coordinate equals −(old x-coordinate): (x, y) → (y, −x).
Check: (−5, 0) → (0, 5) ✓; (−2, 0) → (0, 2) ✓; (−1, 3) → (3, 1) ✓; (−5, 5) → (5, 5) ✓.
By the book's rules, (x, y) → (y, −x) is the rule for a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin.
So the transformation is a rotation through 90° in the clockwise direction about the origin (0, 0).

mcqs.q: What is the rule for a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin?
mcqs.why: The book rule for 90 degrees clockwise about the origin is (x, y) to (y, -x); for example (1, -2) maps to (-2, -1) by this rule.

mcqs.q: What is the rule for a rotation of 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin?
mcqs.why: The book rule for 90 degrees anticlockwise (counterclockwise) about the origin is (x, y) to (-y, x); for example (5, 7) maps to (-7, 5).

mcqs.q: What is the rule for a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin?
mcqs.why: A half turn about the origin changes the sign of both coordinates: (x, y) to (-x, -y); for example (0, -1) maps to (0, 1).

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, what is the image of A(1, -2)?
mcqs.why: Apply (x, y) to (y, -x) with x = 1, y = -2: image = (y, -x) = (-2, -1), exactly as listed in Exercise 4.5 Question 6.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, what is the image of C(3, 2)?
mcqs.why: Apply (x, y) to (y, -x) with x = 3, y = 2: image = (y, -x) = (2, -3), exactly as listed in Exercise 4.5 Question 6.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin, what is the image of P(-1, -5)?
mcqs.why: Apply (x, y) to (-x, -y) with x = -1, y = -5: image = (-(-1), -(-5)) = (1, 5), as listed in Exercise 4.5 Question 7.

mcqs.q: Under a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin, what is the image of S(3, -2)?
mcqs.why: Apply (x, y) to (-x, -y) with x = 3, y = -2: image = (-3, 2), as listed in Exercise 4.5 Question 7.

mcqs.q: A triangle has vertices (0, -1), (-8, -2) and (-4, -5). After a 180-degree rotation about the origin, what is the image of (-8, -2)?
mcqs.why: Apply the half-turn rule (x, y) to (-x, -y): (-8, -2) maps to (8, 2), and the full image triangle is (0, 1), (8, 2), (4, 5).

mcqs.q: Shape QERN maps to Q'E'R'N' by (x, y) to (y, -x), for example Q(-5, 0) to Q'(0, 5). Describe the transformation fully.
options: A rotation of 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin
A rotation of 180 degrees about the origin
A rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about the origin
A reflection in the line y = x
mcqs.why: Check Q: (x, y) = (-5, 0) gives (y, -x) = (0, 5) = Q', and (y, -x) is the book rule for 90 degrees clockwise about the origin (0, 0).

mcqs.q: What happens to a shape under a rotation about a centre of rotation?
options: Every point turns through a different angle
The image is larger than the original
The image is a mirror image of the original
Every point turns through the same angle and the image is congruent to the original
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a rotation every point turns through the same angle about the centre and the image is congruent to the original shape.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.6
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Draw an enlargement of △ABC with vertices A(5, 3), B(3, 3), C(3, 5) and centre of enlargement P(5, 5) with scale factor 2.

For an enlargement, image point = centre + scale factor × (point − centre). Here centre P(5, 5) and scale factor k = 2, so each vertex moves twice as far from P in the same direction.
A(5, 3): A − P = (0, −2); ×2 = (0, −4); A′ = (5, 5 − 4) = (5, 1).
B(3, 3): B − P = (−2, −2); ×2 = (−4, −4); B′ = (1, 1).
C(3, 5): C − P = (−2, 0); ×2 = (−4, 0); C′ = (1, 5).
Construction: draw rays PA, PB, PC from P through each vertex, measure PA, PB, PC with compasses, mark A′ on ray PA with PA′ = 2 × PA, and similarly B′ and C′, then join A′B′C′.
The enlarged triangle A′B′C′ has vertices (5, 1), (1, 1) and (1, 5); each side is twice the corresponding side of △ABC.

Q2. Draw an enlargement of △ABC with vertices A(0, 5), B(1, 1), C(4, 0) and centre of enlargement O with scale factor 1/2.

Centre O is the origin (0, 0) and the scale factor is k = 1/2, so each image point is halfway from O to the original point: (x, y) → (x/2, y/2).
A(0, 5) → A′(0, 2.5).
B(1, 1) → B′(0.5, 0.5).
C(4, 0) → C′(2, 0).
Construction: draw rays OA, OB, OC; mark the midpoint of each (with compasses) as A′, B′, C′ respectively; join A′B′C′.
The image △A′B′C′ has vertices (0, 2.5), (0.5, 0.5) and (2, 0), and is a reduction — each side is half the corresponding side of △ABC.

Q3. In the diagram, △A′B′C′ has been enlarged to give △ABC. A′(2, 5.5), B′(3, 4) and C′(4, 4.5) map to A(1, 5), B(3, 2) and C(5, 3). Calculate the centre of enlargement and state the scale factor of the enlargement.

The centre of enlargement is the point where the lines joining corresponding vertices (AA′, BB′, CC′) all meet.
Line BB′: B(3, 2) and B′(3, 4) both have x = 3, so BB′ is the vertical line x = 3.
Line AA′: from A(1, 5) to A′(2, 5.5) the line rises 0.5 for each 1 step in x; at x = 3 it reaches y = 5 + 2 × 0.5 = 6. So AA′ also passes through (3, 6). Check with CC′: from C(5, 3) to C′(4, 4.5), at x = 3 the line reaches y = 3 + 2 × 1.5 = 6 ✓. So the centre of enlargement is (3, 6).
Scale factor = distance from centre to image point ÷ distance from centre to object point. Using B: centre (3, 6) to B(3, 2) is 4 units; centre to B′(3, 4) is 2 units. Since A′B′C′ was enlarged to give ABC, scale factor = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
So the centre of enlargement is (3, 6) and the scale factor is 2.

Q4. Draw an enlargement of △ABC with vertices A(1, 4), B(3, 4) and C(3, 1) and centre of enlargement the origin with scale factor −2.

With centre the origin and scale factor k = −2, each point (x, y) maps to (−2x, −2y). The negative sign puts the image on the opposite side of the centre, and the image is twice as large.
A(1, 4) → A′(−2, −8).
B(3, 4) → B′(−6, −8).
C(3, 1) → C′(−6, −2).
Construction: draw the ray from O through A and produce it backwards through O; mark A′ on the produced ray with OA′ = 2 × OA. Do the same for B′ and C′, then join A′B′C′.
The image △A′B′C′ has vertices (−2, −8), (−6, −8) and (−6, −2), in the third quadrant.

Q5. Draw an enlargement of the shaded shape shown with scale factor 3 and centre of enlargement the marked point. (Figure: a shaded right angled triangle on squared paper, its vertices lying 2, 3 and 3 grid units from the marked centre point)

Working (ray method, book Example of enlargement):
Step 1: From the centre of enlargement O, draw rays through each vertex of the shaded triangle.
Step 2: Measure the distance from O to each vertex with a ruler or compasses (on the grid the three vertices lie at displacements (2, 2), (3, 2) and (3, 0) grid units from O, reading the printed grid).
Step 3: Multiply each distance by the scale factor 3: the image vertices lie at displacements (6, 6), (9, 6) and (9, 0) grid units from O, on the same rays. Mark them A′, B′, C′.
Step 4: Join A′B′C′.
The image is a right angled triangle similar to the shaded one with every side 3 times as long, in the same direction from O. (Displacements were read from the printed grid and are accurate to the grid squares.)

Q6. Find the scale factor of enlargement used to enlarge shape A to shape B. (Figure: shape A is an L-shaped block 3 units wide and 3 units high; shape B is the same L-shape 9 units wide and 9 units high)

Scale factor = length on the image ÷ corresponding length on the object.
Width: shape B is 9 units wide and shape A is 3 units wide, so scale factor = 9 ÷ 3 = 3.
Check with the height: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 ✓ (the vertical parts also measure 3 units in A and 9 units in B).
So the scale factor of the enlargement is 3.

Q7. Find the scale factor of the enlargement that maps shape X onto shape Y. (Figure: shape X is a block shape 2 units high and 4 units wide; shape Y is the same shape 4 units high and 8 units wide)

Scale factor = length on the image (Y) ÷ corresponding length on the object (X).
Height: Y is 4 units high and X is 2 units high, so scale factor = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Check with the width: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 ✓.
So the scale factor of the enlargement is 2.

Q8. Draw an enlargement of square ABCD with vertices A(9, 3), B(15, 3), C(15, 9) and D(9, 9) and centre of enlargement the origin with scale factor −1/3.

With centre the origin and scale factor k = −1/3, each point (x, y) maps to (−x/3, −y/3). The image is smaller, inverted, and on the opposite side of the origin.
A(9, 3) → A′(−3, −1).
B(15, 3) → B′(−5, −1).
C(15, 9) → C′(−5, −3).
D(9, 9) → D′(−3, −3).
Construction: draw rays from O through each vertex and produce them backwards; mark each image point at one third of the original distance from O on the opposite side; join A′B′C′D′.
The image is the square A′B′C′D′ with side 2 units (the original side 6 units × 1/3), in the third quadrant.

Q9. Find the centre of enlargement for this transformation. (Figure: a small flag shape and its enlarged image on a coordinate grid, with rays through corresponding vertices meeting at the origin)

Draw (or extend) the lines joining each vertex of the small flag to the corresponding vertex of its image.
All of these joining lines pass through one common point.
From the printed figure, the joining lines meet at the origin of the grid.
So the centre of enlargement is the origin, (0, 0). (The image lies on the opposite side of the centre and is smaller, so the scale factor is negative, about −1/2; the question asks only for the centre.)

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has A(5, 3), B(3, 3), C(3, 5), centre P(5, 5) and scale factor 2. What is the image of A?
mcqs.why: A - P = (5-5, 3-5) = (0, -2); multiply by 2 gives (0, -4); add P: (5, 5-4) = (5, 1), using image = centre + k times (point - centre).

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has A(5, 3), B(3, 3), C(3, 5), centre P(5, 5) and scale factor 2. What is the image of B?
Triangle ABC has A(0, 5), B(1, 1), C(4, 0), centre the origin and scale factor 1/2. What is the image of C?
mcqs.why: With centre the origin, (x, y) goes to (x/2, y/2): C(4, 0) maps to (4/2, 0/2) = (2, 0), and the image is a reduction to half size.

mcqs.q: An enlargement maps A'(2, 5.5), B'(3, 4), C'(4, 4.5) to A(1, 5), B(3, 2), C(5, 3). What is the centre of enlargement?
mcqs.why: Line BB' is x = 3 since B(3, 2) and B'(3, 4) share x = 3; line AA' reaches y = 5 + 2 x 0.5 = 6 at x = 3, so the joining lines meet at (3, 6).

mcqs.q: In the enlargement where B'(3, 4) maps to B(3, 2) with centre (3, 6), what is the scale factor?
mcqs.why: Scale factor = centre-to-image distance / centre-to-object distance = distance (3,6) to (3,2) / distance (3,6) to (3,4) = 4 / 2 = 2.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has A(1, 4), B(3, 4), C(3, 1), centre the origin and scale factor -2. What is the image of A?
mcqs.why: With centre the origin and k = -2, (x, y) goes to (-2x, -2y): A(1, 4) maps to (-2 x 1, -2 x 4) = (-2, -8), on the opposite side of the centre.

mcqs.q: Shape A is an L-shape 3 units wide and shape B is the same L-shape 9 units wide. What is the scale factor from A to B?
mcqs.why: Scale factor = image length / object length = width of B / width of A = 9 / 3 = 3, confirmed by the heights 9 / 3 = 3 as well.

mcqs.q: Shape X is 2 units high and 4 units wide; shape Y is 4 units high and 8 units wide. What is the scale factor from X to Y?
mcqs.why: Scale factor = image length / object length = height of Y / height of X = 4 / 2 = 2, confirmed by the widths 8 / 4 = 2.

mcqs.q: Square ABCD has A(9, 3) and side 6 units. With centre the origin and scale factor -1/3, what is the side length of the image square?
mcqs.why: Image side = original side x |scale factor| = 6 x 1/3 = 2 units; for example A(9, 3) maps to (-3, -1) and B(15, 3) to (-5, -1), a distance of 2.

mcqs.q: What does a negative scale factor tell you about an enlargement?
options: The image lies on the same side of the centre
The image lies on the opposite side of the centre from the object
The image is always smaller than the object
The image is a reflection with no size change
mcqs.why: With k = -2 or k = -1/3 in the notes, each point maps to the opposite side of the centre, e.g. (1, 4) to (-2, -8), because the sign is negative.

lessons.title: Exercise 5.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. The marks of a student Zeeshan in the grade 6 examinations were 50, 80, 60, 50, 85, 90. Show these marks by drawing an appropriate graph.

The data is discrete (marks in six examinations), so a bar graph is appropriate, as in the book a bar graph is used for discrete data.
Write the data in order: Paper 1: 50, Paper 2: 80, Paper 3: 60, Paper 4: 50, Paper 5: 85, Paper 6: 90 (the book does not name the papers, so they are taken in the order given).
Draw two axes: the examinations (papers) on the x-axis and the marks on the y-axis.
Choose a scale on the y-axis: 1 square represents 10 marks, so the y-axis runs 0, 10, 20, ..., 100.
Draw a bar of height 50 for Paper 1, a bar of height 80 for Paper 2, a bar of height 60 for Paper 3, a bar of height 50 for Paper 4, a bar of height 85 for Paper 5 and a bar of height 90 for Paper 6. All bars have the same width and equal gaps.
Give the graph the title: Graph showing the marks of Zeeshan in the grade 6 examinations.
Reading the finished graph: the tallest bar is Paper 6 (90 marks, the highest) and the shortest bars are Paper 1 and Paper 4 (50 marks each, the lowest).

Q2. A shopkeeper sold the following number of toys in 6 weeks. Weeks: I: 120, II: 80, III: 90, IV: 125, V: 110, VI: 75. Represent the above information by a simple bar graph. Also tell: (i) How many toys were sold by the shopkeeper altogether? (ii) In which week the maximum and least number of toys were sold?

Draw two axes: the weeks I, II, III, IV, V, VI on the x-axis and the number of toys on the y-axis.
Choose a scale on the y-axis: 1 square represents 10 toys.
Draw bars of heights: Week I: 120, Week II: 80, Week III: 90, Week IV: 125, Week V: 110, Week VI: 75. All bars have the same width.
Give the graph the title: Graph showing the number of toys sold in 6 weeks.
(i) Total toys sold = 120 + 80 + 90 + 125 + 110 + 75.
Add step by step: 120 + 80 = 200; 200 + 90 = 290; 290 + 125 = 415; 415 + 110 = 525; 525 + 75 = 600.
So altogether 600 toys were sold.
(ii) The tallest bar is Week IV with 125 toys, so the maximum number of toys was sold in Week IV.
The shortest bar is Week VI with 75 toys, so the least number of toys was sold in Week VI.

Q3. Draw an appropriate graph to show the points out of 100 scored by four students in three games. Ali: Game-I 72, Game-II 60, Game-III 85. Anam: Game-I 48, Game-II 50, Game-III 75. Zara: Game-I 80, Game-II 30, Game-III 60. Umer: Game-I 50, Game-II 80, Game-III 50.

Three values are to be compared for each student, so a multiple bar graph is appropriate (the book uses a multiple bar graph for comparison of two or more characteristics).
Draw two axes: the students Ali, Anam, Zara, Umer in groups on the x-axis and the points (out of 100) on the y-axis.
Choose a scale on the y-axis: 1 square represents 10 points, from 0 to 100.
For Ali draw three bars side by side of heights 72 (Game-I), 60 (Game-II) and 85 (Game-III), using a different shading for each game, as shown in the key.
For Anam draw three bars of heights 48, 50 and 75. For Zara draw three bars of heights 80, 30 and 60. For Umer draw three bars of heights 50, 80 and 50.
Add a key: first shading = Game-I, second shading = Game-II, third shading = Game-III, and give the title: Graph showing the points scored by four students in three games.
Reading the graph: the highest single score is Ali in Game-III (85 points) and the lowest single score is Zara in Game-II (30 points).

Q4. The following are the runs made in a two days cricket match by the students in a high school. Draw an appropriate graph for the following data. Javed: 1st day 55, 2nd day 90. Hamza: 1st day 60, 2nd day 25. Husnain: 1st day 35, 2nd day 45. Jamshaid: 1st day 80, 2nd day 50. Arsalan: 1st day 65, 2nd day 30.

Two values (1st day and 2nd day) are to be compared for each player, so a multiple bar graph is appropriate.
Draw two axes: the players Javed, Hamza, Husnain, Jamshaid, Arsalan in groups on the x-axis and the runs on the y-axis.
Choose a scale on the y-axis: 1 square represents 10 runs, from 0 to 100.
For each player draw two bars side by side: Javed 55 and 90; Hamza 60 and 25; Husnain 35 and 45; Jamshaid 80 and 50; Arsalan 65 and 30. Use one shading for the 1st day and another for the 2nd day and show them in a key.
Give the graph the title: Graph showing the runs made by the students in a two days cricket match.
Reading the graph: the highest score is Javed on the 2nd day (90 runs) and the lowest score is Hamza on the 2nd day (25 runs).

Q5. Mrs. Imran purchased the following goods and services from a grocery store for her kitchen in the last month. Graph the data using a pie graph. Rice: Rs. 600, Flour: Rs. 500, Sugar: Rs. 300, Soap: Rs. 150, Oil: Rs. 800, Miscellaneous: Rs. 250 (expenditure in Rs.).

For a pie graph, first find the total expenditure: Total = 600 + 500 + 300 + 150 + 800 + 250 = Rs. 2600.
The angle of each sector is found by the formula: Angle = (expenditure of the item / total expenditure) × 360 degrees.
Rice: (600 / 2600) × 360 = 83.08 degrees, about 83.1 degrees.
Flour: (500 / 2600) × 360 = 69.23 degrees, about 69.2 degrees.
Sugar: (300 / 2600) × 360 = 41.54 degrees, about 41.5 degrees.
Soap: (150 / 2600) × 360 = 20.77 degrees, about 20.8 degrees.
Oil: (800 / 2600) × 360 = 110.77 degrees, about 110.8 degrees.
Miscellaneous: (250 / 2600) × 360 = 34.62 degrees, about 34.6 degrees.
Check: 83.1 + 69.2 + 41.5 + 20.8 + 110.8 + 34.6 = 360.0 degrees, as required.
Draw a circle and, using a protractor, mark the sectors of 83.1 degrees (Rice), 69.2 degrees (Flour), 41.5 degrees (Sugar), 20.8 degrees (Soap), 110.8 degrees (Oil) and 34.6 degrees (Miscellaneous). Label each sector. The largest sector is Oil, the biggest item of expenditure.

Q6. A shirt making company prepared the following number of shirts with different colours. Draw a pie chart for the following data: Red: 50, Blue: 60, Green: 35, Black: 40, White: 70, Yellow: 80 (number of shirts).

First find the total number of shirts: Total = 50 + 60 + 35 + 40 + 70 + 80 = 335 shirts.
The angle of each sector is found by the formula: Angle = (number of shirts of the colour / total shirts) × 360 degrees.
Red: (50 / 335) × 360 = 53.73 degrees, about 53.7 degrees.
Blue: (60 / 335) × 360 = 64.48 degrees, about 64.5 degrees.
Green: (35 / 335) × 360 = 37.61 degrees, about 37.6 degrees.
Black: (40 / 335) × 360 = 42.99 degrees, about 43.0 degrees.
White: (70 / 335) × 360 = 75.22 degrees, about 75.2 degrees.
Yellow: (80 / 335) × 360 = 85.97 degrees, about 86.0 degrees.
Check: 53.7 + 64.5 + 37.6 + 43.0 + 75.2 + 86.0 = 360.0 degrees, as required.
Draw a circle and mark the six sectors with a protractor, labelling each sector with its colour. The largest sector is Yellow (80 shirts) and the smallest sector is Green (35 shirts).

Q7. A factory makes fertilizer and sold in 5 cities i.e., 15% sold in city A, 20% sold in city B, 25% sold in city C, 35% sold in city D and 5% sold in city E. Draw a suitable graph to represent this information.

Percentages of a total are best shown by a pie chart, so a pie graph is the suitable graph.
Convert each percentage into a sector angle by the formula: Angle = (percentage / 100) × 360 degrees.
City A: (15 / 100) × 360 = 54 degrees.
City B: (20 / 100) × 360 = 72 degrees.
City C: (25 / 100) × 360 = 90 degrees.
City D: (35 / 100) × 360 = 126 degrees.
City E: (5 / 100) × 360 = 18 degrees.
Check: 54 + 72 + 90 + 126 + 18 = 360 degrees, and 15 + 20 + 25 + 35 + 5 = 100%, as required.
Draw a circle and mark the sectors of 54 degrees (A), 72 degrees (B), 90 degrees (C), 126 degrees (D) and 18 degrees (E) with a protractor. Label each sector. The largest sale is in city D (35%) and the smallest in city E (5%).

Q8. The distribution of masses (lbs) of 100 students is given. Draw a suitable graph to represent the data. Midpoints of masses: 114.5, 124.5, 134.5, 144.5, 154.5, 164.5. Frequency: 35, 20, 10, 5, 15, 15.

The data is continuous (masses with midpoints and frequencies), so a histogram and a frequency polygon are suitable, as in the book continuous data is mostly represented by histogram and frequency polygon.
The gap between consecutive midpoints is 10, so each class has width 10. Taking half the width (5) on each side of a midpoint gives the class boundaries: 109.5-119.5, 119.5-129.5, 129.5-139.5, 139.5-149.5, 149.5-159.5, 159.5-169.5.
The classes with their frequencies are: 109.5-119.5: 35, 119.5-129.5: 20, 129.5-139.5: 10, 139.5-149.5: 5, 149.5-159.5: 15, 159.5-169.5: 15. Check: 35 + 20 + 10 + 5 + 15 + 15 = 100 students.
Histogram: draw the class boundaries on the x-axis and the frequencies on the y-axis, and draw touching bars (no gaps) of heights 35, 20, 10, 5, 15 and 15 over the six classes.
Frequency polygon: plot the points (114.5, 35), (124.5, 20), (134.5, 10), (144.5, 5), (154.5, 15), (164.5, 15), i.e. each midpoint against its frequency, and join the points by straight line segments in order.
Reading the graph: the tallest bar is the first class (midpoint 114.5 lbs, 35 students), so most students have masses near 114.5 lbs, and the shortest bar is the class with midpoint 144.5 lbs (only 5 students).

mcqs.q: Zeeshan's marks were 50, 80, 60, 50, 85, 90. Which type of graph is appropriate for this discrete data?
mcqs.why: The notes state a bar graph is used for discrete data such as marks in six examinations, with equal-width bars and a scale of 1 square for 10 marks.

mcqs.q: A shopkeeper sold 120, 80, 90, 125, 110 and 75 toys in weeks I to VI. How many toys were sold altogether?
Toys sold in weeks I to VI were 120, 80, 90, 125, 110, 75. In which week were the most toys sold?
mcqs.why: Compare the bar heights: the largest value is 125 in Week IV, greater than 120, 110, 90, 80 and 75, so the maximum was sold in Week IV.

mcqs.q: Toys sold in weeks I to VI were 120, 80, 90, 125, 110, 75. In which week were the fewest toys sold?
mcqs.why: Compare the bar heights: the smallest value is 75 in Week VI, less than 80, 90, 110, 120 and 125, so the least was sold in Week VI.

mcqs.q: Four students scored in three games. What is the highest single score and who scored it?
mcqs.why: Scanning all twelve scores (72, 60, 85, 48, 50, 75, 80, 30, 60, 50, 80, 50), the maximum is 85, scored by Ali in Game-III in the multiple bar graph.

mcqs.q: Mrs Imran spent Rs 600, 500, 300, 150, 800, 250 on six items. What is the total expenditure for the pie graph?
mcqs.why: Total = 600 + 500 + 300 + 150 + 800 + 250 = 2600, so Rs 2600 is the denominator in Angle = (item / total) x 360 for every sector.

mcqs.q: Mrs Imran spent Rs 800 on Oil out of a total of Rs 2600. What is the pie sector angle for Oil?
mcqs.why: Angle = (expenditure / total) x 360 = (800 / 2600) x 360 = 0.3077 x 360 = 110.77, about 110.8 degrees, the largest sector.

mcqs.q: A shirt company made 50 red, 60 blue, 35 green, 40 black, 70 white and 80 yellow shirts. How many shirts were made in total?
mcqs.why: Total = 50 + 60 + 35 + 40 + 70 + 80 = 335 shirts, so 335 is the denominator in Angle = (colour count / total) x 360.

mcqs.q: Fertilizer sales were 15% in city A, 20% in B, 25% in C, 35% in D and 5% in E. What is the pie sector angle for city C?
mcqs.why: Angle = (percentage / 100) x 360 = (25 / 100) x 360 = 0.25 x 360 = 90 degrees for city C; city D gives 126 degrees and city A gives 54 degrees.

mcqs.q: Masses of 100 students have midpoints 114.5 to 164.5 with frequencies 35, 20, 10, 5, 15, 15. Which graphs are suitable for this continuous data?
options: A histogram and a frequency polygon
mcqs.why: The notes state continuous data is mostly represented by histogram and frequency polygon; here frequencies sum to 35+20+10+5+15+15 = 100 students.

lessons.title: Exercise 5.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. The following data displays the number of draws of different categories of bonds. 35, 55, 64, 70, 99, 89, 87, 65, 67, 38, 62, 60, 70, 78, 69, 86, 39, 71, 56, 75, 51, 99, 68, 95, 86, 53, 59, 50, 47, 55, 81, 80, 98, 51, 63, 66, 79, 85, 83, 70. Construct a frequency distribution and cumulative frequency distribution for the above data, with seven classes of equal size of class interval 10.

Count the values: there are 40 values. The smallest value is 35 and the largest value is 99.
Seven classes of width 10 starting from 31-40 cover the whole data: 31-40, 41-50, 51-60, 61-70, 71-80, 81-90, 91-100.
Count the values in 31-40 by tally marks: 35, 38, 39 give frequency f = 3. Cumulative frequency c.f. = 3.
Count the values in 41-50: 47, 50 give f = 2. c.f. = 3 + 2 = 5.
Count the values in 51-60: 55, 56, 51, 53, 59, 51, 55, 60 give f = 8. c.f. = 5 + 8 = 13.
Count the values in 61-70: 64, 70, 65, 67, 62, 70, 69, 68, 63, 66, 70 give f = 11. c.f. = 13 + 11 = 24.
Count the values in 71-80: 78, 71, 75, 80, 79 give f = 5. c.f. = 24 + 5 = 29.
Count the values in 81-90: 89, 87, 86, 86, 81, 85, 83 give f = 7. c.f. = 29 + 7 = 36.
Count the values in 91-100: 99, 99, 95, 98 give f = 4. c.f. = 36 + 4 = 40.
Frequency distribution (class: f, c.f.): 31-40: 3, 3; 41-50: 2, 5; 51-60: 8, 13; 61-70: 11, 24; 71-80: 5, 29; 81-90: 7, 36; 91-100: 4, 40. Check: total frequency = 3 + 2 + 8 + 11 + 5 + 7 + 4 = 40, equal to the number of values.

Q2. Listed below are the number of electricity units consumed by 50 households in a low income group in a locality of Lahore. 55, 45, 64, 130, 66, 155, 80, 102, 62, 60, 101, 58, 75, 81, 111, 90, 55, 151, 66, 139, 77, 99, 67, 51, 50, 125, 83, 55, 136, 91, 86, 54, 78, 100, 113, 93, 104, 111, 113, 96, 96, 87, 109, 94, 129, 99, 69, 83, 97, 97. With 12 classes of equal width of 10, construct a frequency and cumulative frequency distribution for the electricity units consumed.

Count the values: there are 50 values. The smallest value is 45 and the largest value is 155.
Twelve classes of width 10 starting from 41-50 cover the whole data: 41-50, 51-60, 61-70, 71-80, 81-90, 91-100, 101-110, 111-120, 121-130, 131-140, 141-150, 151-160.
41-50: values 45, 50 give f = 2, c.f. = 2. 51-60: values 55, 58, 55, 51, 54, 55, 60 give f = 7, c.f. = 2 + 7 = 9.
61-70: values 64, 66, 62, 66, 67, 69 give f = 6, c.f. = 9 + 6 = 15. 71-80: values 80, 75, 77, 78 give f = 4, c.f. = 15 + 4 = 19.
81-90: values 81, 90, 83, 86, 87, 83 give f = 6, c.f. = 19 + 6 = 25. 91-100: values 99, 91, 100, 93, 96, 96, 94, 99, 97, 97 give f = 10, c.f. = 25 + 10 = 35.
101-110: values 102, 101, 104, 109 give f = 4, c.f. = 35 + 4 = 39. 111-120: values 111, 111, 113, 113 give f = 4, c.f. = 39 + 4 = 43.
121-130: values 130, 125, 129 give f = 3, c.f. = 43 + 3 = 46. 131-140: values 139, 136 give f = 2, c.f. = 46 + 2 = 48.
141-150: no value falls in this class, so f = 0, c.f. = 48 + 0 = 48. 151-160: values 155, 151 give f = 2, c.f. = 48 + 2 = 50.
Frequency distribution (class: f, c.f.): 41-50: 2, 2; 51-60: 7, 9; 61-70: 6, 15; 71-80: 4, 19; 81-90: 6, 25; 91-100: 10, 35; 101-110: 4, 39; 111-120: 4, 43; 121-130: 3, 46; 131-140: 2, 48; 141-150: 0, 48; 151-160: 2, 50. Check: total frequency = 50, equal to the number of households.
Note: In the printed Answers the total row of this table is misprinted as total frequency 40; the printed class frequencies themselves add to 50, which is the correct total for 50 households.

Q3. The following list is of scores in a mathematics examination. Using the starting class 40-44, set up a frequency and cumulative frequency distribution. List the class boundaries. 63, 88, 79, 92, 86, 87, 83, 78, 40, 67, 68, 76, 46, 81, 92, 77, 84, 76, 70, 66, 77, 75, 98, 81, 82, 81, 87, 78, 70, 60, 94, 79, 52, 82, 77, 81.

Count the values: there are 36 scores. With class width 5 and starting class 40-44, the classes are: 40-44, 45-49, 50-54, 55-59, 60-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, 90-94, 95-99.
Class boundaries are obtained by subtracting 0.5 from each lower limit and adding 0.5 to each upper limit: 39.5-44.5, 44.5-49.5, 49.5-54.5, 54.5-59.5, 59.5-64.5, 64.5-69.5, 69.5-74.5, 74.5-79.5, 79.5-84.5, 84.5-89.5, 89.5-94.5, 94.5-99.5.
40-44: value 40 gives f = 1, c.f. = 1. 45-49: value 46 gives f = 1, c.f. = 1 + 1 = 2. 50-54: value 52 gives f = 1, c.f. = 2 + 1 = 3. 55-59: no value, f = 0, c.f. = 3.
60-64: values 63, 60 give f = 2, c.f. = 3 + 2 = 5. 65-69: values 67, 68, 66 give f = 3, c.f. = 5 + 3 = 8. 70-74: values 70, 70 give f = 2, c.f. = 8 + 2 = 10.

For a frequency polygon, take the midpoints on the x-axis, put a dot against each midpoint at the height of its class frequency, and join all the dots by line segments.
